USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue intensive negotiations while maintaining current tariff levels as leverage. Do not escalate further — the talks are close to a deal. Do not prematurely remove all tariffs — preserve enforcement leverage. Push hard on structural issues (IP, forced tech transfer, enforcement mechanism) while being flexible on the pace of tariff removal as compliance is demonstrated.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading of +0.25 reflects a situation where the US faces real but manageable costs from the trade war. The US economy is slowing (Q4 2018 GDP at 2.2%, Fed projecting 2.1% for 2019, down from 2.3% in December), 10Y Treasury yields have fallen sharply from 3.24% to 2.53% signaling growth concerns, and the Fed has paused rate hikes. The Beige Book (April 17) reports trade uncertainty constraining business investment in several districts, and farmers remain under significant stress from Chinese retaliation on ~$110B of US agricultural exports. However, the US economy remains fundamentally strong — unemployment at 3.7% (near 50-year low), inflation contained at 1.8% PCE, and the labor market is tight.

The action score of +0.1 (negotiate) reflects the current leverage position. The US holds significant advantages: tariffs on $250B of Chinese goods give enforcement leverage; China's economy is slowing more sharply (6.4% Q1 2019, slowest since 1992, with record stimulus needed); and China has made 'unprecedented proposals' on forced technology transfer (US officials, March 28). Enforcement mechanism and tariff removal remain the two key sticking points (LA Times, April 23; CNBC, April 2). Trump himself said a deal could come 'in weeks' (Politico, April 5). Escalation now would be counterproductive — it would destabilize markets, hurt US consumers and farmers further, and risk collapsing talks that are near completion. But premature concession (removing all tariffs) would surrender enforcement leverage before China has demonstrated compliance on structural reforms. The optimal stance is to negotiate firmly, maintain tariff leverage, and push for a deal with robust enforcement — including the right to reimpose tariffs unilaterally if China violates commitments.
key_factors: US tariffs on $250B of Chinese goods provide significant negotiation leverage
China economy slowing to 6.4% Q1 (slowest since 1992), requiring record stimulus
US economy moderating but strong: 3.7% unemployment, 2.1% projected GDP growth
Enforcement mechanism and tariff removal are final sticking points in negotiations
China made 'unprecedented proposals' on forced tech transfer (late March)
10Y Treasury yield decline (3.24% to 2.53%) signals market concern about growth
US farmers suffering from Chinese retaliation on agricultural exports
Both sides motivated to close deal — Trump says 'weeks away' (April 5)

sources_cited.excerpt: Intensive Washington talks between US and Chinese negotiators; both sides report progress on text, including enforcement language. No final deal signed.
List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5-10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
Trump said a 'monumental' agreement could come in the next four weeks. 'We've negotiated out some of the tougher points. But we have some ways to go.'
China made unprecedented proposals on forced technology transfer. 'They're talking about forced technology transfer in a way that they've never wanted to talk about before.'
Tariffs are one of the last big obstacles. China wants duties lifted; US wants to leave at least some in place as enforcement leverage.
Federal funds rate at 2.42%, up 22bp over 6 months but Fed has paused further hikes.
10Y Treasury yield fallen from 3.24% (Nov 2018) to 2.53% (April 2019), a 71bp decline signaling growth concerns.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue negotiating actively toward a deal, but resist accepting an asymmetric enforcement mechanism that gives the US unilateral snapback tariff rights without reciprocal recourse. Seek a face-saving framework that includes genuine structural concessions on IP and market access while preserving China's policy sovereignty. No new escalation — the domestic economy needs stability, and the current trajectory favors patience.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE:

Threat Score (+0.45 — moderate-to-high, between neutral and high threat):

(a) The tariff burden is real and material. US Section 301 tariffs cover ~$250B of Chinese imports (Lists 1-3 at 25%/25%/10%). The List 3 rate remains suspended at 10% but could snap to 25% if talks collapse (timeline entry: 2018-09-17, 2018-12-01). China's retaliatory tariffs on ~$101B of US exports have costs too, but the asymmetry matters: China exports far more to the US than it imports, so tariff escalation hits China harder in absolute terms.

(b) Manufacturing stress is evident. The official PMI contracted for three consecutive months (Dec 2018–Feb 2019), reaching its lowest level since 2009. Export orders sub-index hit a decade low in February 2019. The frontloading effect that boosted 2018 exports has worn off (The Diplomat, March 2019; Reuters, Dec 2018).

(c) The Huawei/Meng situation is an active escalation vector. DOJ unsealed fraud and sanctions charges (Jan 28, 2019). Canada authorized extradition proceedings (March 1). This could expand into broader entity-list restrictions on Chinese tech firms, threatening China's technology ambitions — a core strategic interest. China's retaliatory detention of two Canadians (Dec 10, 2018) signals the situation is already tit-for-tat.

(d) However, China's economy is showing resilience. Q1 2019 GDP beat expectations at 6.4% YoY (SCMP, April 17). March industrial production surged 8.5% YoY — strongest since July 2014. Stimulus (8.2T yuan in Q1 credit) is working. This means China is not in crisis mode and has room to negotiate from a position of relative stability rather than desperation.

(e) The threat is not yet existential because: (i) the economy is stabilizing; (ii) talks are progressing — Mnuchin said April 10 the enforcement mechanism is 'pretty much agreed'; (iii) the tariff hike has been repeatedly delayed; and (iv) China retains retaliatory capacity and can diversify trade relationships over time. But it is above neutral because the enforcement mechanism question could lock China into an unfavorable structural arrangement.

Action Score (+0.05 — negotiate, very slightly toward concession):

(a) The talks are in their final stretch. Both sides have made progress on text, including enforcement language (timeline: April 3). Walking away now would be worse than continuing — it would trigger the List 3 hike to 25%, potentially additional tariffs on remaining ~$300B of imports, and possible Huawei entity-list escalation. The cost of collapse is high.

(b) But China should not accept the emerging US demand for unilateral snapback rights. Lighthizer has stated the US must maintain the right to reimpose tariffs 'in situations where there's violations of the agreement' without China being able to retaliate (NYT, April 11). This is effectively permanent US leverage over China's economy — an asymmetric enforcement mechanism that would undermine China's sovereignty. Xi Jinping himself stated on Dec 18: 'No one is in a position to dictate to the Chinese people what should or should not be done.'

(c) The optimal strategy is to accept genuine structural concessions (IP protection, market access, currency transparency) that China can implement domestically — these are reforms China arguably needs anyway — while insisting on symmetric enforcement. If the US can snap back tariffs, China must retain reciprocal rights. This is a deal China can sell domestically as a win-win rather than a capitulation.

(d) China's Q1 economic strength gives it negotiating leverage. The stimulus is working, the economy is stabilizing, and China does not face an imminent crisis. This means there is no urgent need to accept bad terms. The US, by contrast, faces its own costs: falling 10Y yields (from 3.08% to 2.53%), farm-belt pain from Chinese retaliation on soybeans, and political pressure heading into the 2020 election cycle.

(e) Second-order considerations: accepting an asymmetric deal would set a precedent for future US-China interactions and signal weakness. Rejecting a deal entirely would invite escalation and hurt export-dependent regions. The middle path — negotiate hard on enforcement symmetry while accepting substantive reforms — maximizes China's long-term position.
key_factors: US tariffs cover ~$250B of Chinese imports; List 3 hike to 25% suspended but could resume
China Q1 2019 GDP at 6.4% — stimulus working, economy stabilizing
Manufacturing PMI contracted 3 straight months; export orders at decade low
Huawei/Meng extradition proceedings active; potential for entity-list escalation
Enforcement mechanism is key sticking point — US demands unilateral snapback rights
US 10Y yields fell from 3.08% to 2.53% — US also faces economic costs
China retains significant retaliatory capacity on US agricultural exports

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump directs USTR to finalize List 3: 10% tariffs on ~$200B of Chinese imports effective Sept 24, scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019.
G20 Buenos Aires dinner: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window. Planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended.
Intensive Washington talks between US and Chinese negotiators; both sides report progress on text, including enforcement language.
China's GDP expanded 6.4% in Q1 2019, beating analysts' expectations of 6.3%. Industrial production expanded 8.5% in March — strongest growth since July 2014.
Manufacturing PMI has reached its lowest levels since 2009. Export orders subindex fell to a decade low in February 2019.
China's factory activity contracted for the first time in over two years in December (PMI 49.4). New export orders shrank for a seventh straight month.
The United States is pushing for a broad commitment that would allow American tariffs on Chinese goods to snap back if China violates key promises — without permitting China to retaliate in response.
Mnuchin: We've pretty much agreed on an enforcement mechanism. We've agreed that both sides will establish enforcement offices.
10Y Treasury yield fell from 3.08% (Oct 29) to 2.53% (Apr 24), a decline of 55bp.
